notes.ssebo: Lokapolon, from ekapolon, a leader or elder.
notes.nnyabo: Toto is mother; it is also polite for any woman.

guidebook.intro: Ateso is an Eastern Nilotic language, a cousin of Karimojong and Turkana, not of Luganda. Nouns have no classes, but most start with a vowel that shows gender, and the person is a short prefix on the verb. Start with the greetings used every day.

tips.title: Yoga! Ijai bo?
body: **Yoga** is hello, at any time of day. Follow it with **Ijai bo?** (are you there? how are you?) and answer **Ejai** or **Ejai ejok** (it is well). **Bo** at the end turns a sentence into a question.
In the morning ask **Iperit bo?** (did you sleep?) and answer **Aperit ejok**. **Eyalama** is thank you; **Eyalama noi** is thank you very much.

tips.title: How Ateso sounds
body: **ŋ** is the sound in “singer”, even at the start of a word: **ŋai** (who). **c** is like the “ch” in church: **ecai** (tea). Vowels are as in Spanish or Italian.
Ateso has tone and a set of “whispered” final vowels that written Ateso does not mark, so listen and copy the recordings.

culture.title: Eyalama kanuka aswam
body: **Eyalama kanuka aswam** (thanks for the work) greets anyone who is busy, from a farmer to a shopkeeper. Call an older or unknown man **lokapolon** (sir) and a woman **toto** (mother, madam).
